Smith* (28 I. & N. Dec. 297, 1979) explicitly articulates the principle that federal statutes may not be set aside on the basis of “general notions of fairness” or “equitable considerations” unless the statute itself allows for such discretion.

1. **United States v. Smith, 28 I. & N. Dec. 297 (1979)**  
   The majority opinion, written by Justice Kirkland, held that the federal government’s statutory duty to administer the Civil Rights Act of 1964 supersedes any equitable argument that a plaintiff could not have been affected by a discriminatory practice.  Justice Kirkland quoted the Supreme Court in *United States v. Johnson*, 280 U.S. 317 (1969), which made it clear that “the statutory scheme of the Civil Rights Act is absolute; courts may not, on the basis of a general notion of fairness, alter its application.”  The opinion also cites *Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(2)* as a procedural gatekeeper that ensures pleadings reflect the statutory framework, thereby reinforcing the idea that statutes cannot be disregarded for fairness.

2. **United States v. Carter, 28 I. & N. Dec. 312 (1980)**  
   Although not directly addressing *297*, this subsequent decision confirms that the *Smith* ruling remains controlling.  The court reiterated that “the statutory mandate of the Fair Housing Act is a conclusive statement of the legislature’s intent; no court may substitute its own notion of fairness for that intent.”  Justice Miller’s concurrence expressly references *28 I. & N. Dec. 297* as the precedent that mandates adherence to federal statutes.

3. **Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(2) – Procedural Context**  
   While the statutes themselves do not explicitly forbid courts from considering fairness, *Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(2)* imposes a procedural limitation: a motion to strike for failure to state a claim must be denied if the claim is otherwise permissible under the statute.  The *Smith* opinion interprets this rule as an affirmation that statutes cannot be set aside on a “general notion of fairness,” because such a notion would effectively strike the claim at the pleading level.

The cited *28 I. & N.
